newsitem.title: USA: Martian forecast cold and dusty, but no rain.
newsitem.headline: Martian forecast cold and dusty, but no rain.

text.p: Space officials issued a weather forecast for Mars on Thursday, giving humans the clearest idea yet of the climate on another planet.
Based on images and data sent back from the Pathfinder craft, there are no blue skies over the Red Planet, but plenty of clouds, although don't expect it to ever rain.

Sounding like a TV weatherman, Pathfinder meteorogist Robert Haberle told reporters at a weekly briefing: "The weather report on Mars for sol (Martian day) 26. The pressure is 6.71 millibars and falling. Daytime temperatures are eight degrees above zero Fahrenheit, with winds light from the west."

Continuing the spoof forecast, he added, "We expect continued cool temperatures around 10 degrees F (minus 12.2 C) with overnight lows around minus 105 F (minus 76.1 C), and a chance of late-night or early morning clouds."

More seriously, he said unprecedented readings -- taken every four seconds for a whole day -- show Mars to have a turbulent atmosphere, with major oscillations in air pressure and huge fluctuations in temperatures of 30-40 degrees F in seconds or minutes.
His colleague Mark Lemmon said the pink clouds in the skies over Mars were composed predominantly of dust, but they also contained "waterized particles."
"There is water on Mars, no question," Haberle said. "But it's definitely not liquid -- rather ice or particles. It will definitely not rain on Mars."
"There's a white sun with pink around it at sunset, but no blue sky anywhere on Mars," Lemmon said.

Project scientist Matt Golombek said the data about Mars' atmosphere -- clouds and pressure changes -- were some of the most significant discoveries of the Pathfinder mission, which landed on the planet on July 4.

He said that as the mission neared the end of its first month on Mars, having achieved all its scientific and technological goals, the lander craft would be shut down for two days to recharge its batteries.
"It is near the end of its 30-day life, so we want to recharge it," Golombek said. "After that we will continue day operations."
That means the rover craft Sojourner will continue to drive over the surface, examining soil and rocks with names like "Pooh Bear," "Piglet" and "Mermaid Dune."

But officials at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory here will not be able to conduct night-time operations. "The spacecraft will come to life every day, but it will fall asleep and lose memory at night," said Golombek.

In any case, he said, the Pathfinder mission had achieved everything it was supposed to do in the 30-day planned period on Mars. After recharging the batteries, it will move more into a monitoring mode until it eventually breaks down.
"It will last until something breaks on the rover or the lander," said Golombek. "Something sooner or later will break."
Haberle said he hoped the equipment would last at least another month.
"Currently it's northern summer at the landing site, approaching fall," he said. "Weather systems similar to here on Earth will start moving in from the West in about 30 sols, bringing dust storms."
"We hope Pathfinder lasts long enough to see some of these spectacular storms," said Haberle.
